title: Tax the Penthouse, Not the Payroll
dek: Productive Taxation: We need to fundamentally change how we do taxes
meta: abhi dinesan • april 2026 • taxes, real estate, ai, canada
openingParagraphs: A few weeks ago, Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York dropped a bombshell on New York's upper class with a sharp suit and a cheeky smile that sent every Fox News listener across the five boroughs into a curse-riddled frenzy.
He introduced a pied-à-terre tax - and like all things French, it's expensive and unapologetic in nature.

The idea is that he would impose taxes on luxury second homes owned by non-resident New Yorkers. In doing so, he specifically called out Ken Griffin, CEO of Citadel by posting up outside his $238 million penthouse.
Mamdani’s policy measure was incredibly divisive. And it rallied troops from both sides.

Some folks channeled their inner cannibalist with raging slogans suggesting that we should eat the rich (yuck). Others stood their ground by plainly asserting that "billionaires shouldn’t exist”, an emotional gambit that doesn’t offer much in terms of feasibility or implementation.

Others stood strong in arms behind their billionaire of choice, risking their personal and professional relationships for people that quite frankly, wouldn't look at them twice. Other members of the billi-boys club, like Bill Ackman, jumped in to defend Griffin within hours, because… of course he did.
Not to be pushed around, Citadel hinted it might cut a $6 billion plan to redevelop 350 Park Avenue - a project estimated to create 6,000 construction jobs and 15,000 permanent jobs.

Irrespective of how this shakes out, I can’t help but feel most people are arguing about the wrong thing here. This argument is about how much we should tax rich people. As if rich people are all one black box. That's the entire ceiling of our imagination on this issue.
But this makes a terrible assumption.
And it fundamentally is the wrong way of looking at taxes, at least if we want to reward a productive society.
The actual question is what kind of rich we should be taxing in the first place.

sections.heading: Not Every Rich Person Is the Same
paragraphs: I want to preface this by saying that I’m broke. Like significant negative net worth kinda broke (shoutout Dougy and OSAP loans).

I’m not saying this as a weird flex or sympathetic play, but rather showing that taxing the shit out of billionaires into redistribution checks is probably in my immediate interest. I am definitely not part of the upperclass here.
But, as far as society is concerned, this is bigger than me and this argument is in terms of what’s in everyone’s best interest.
Anyways.

Some rich people are productive members of society. They start businesses, build technological products, employ families, and ultimately drive the future of the world forward. They take risks, they hire people, they create things that didn't exist before. In many ways, they improve the quality of life for everyone and allow people to live a materially better life than the generation(s) before them.

Other rich people extract from society. They contribute to wealth inequality without contributing to wealth creation. They make their money by sitting on top of finite resources and waiting for someone else to be born to make them more valuable.
The best example of this is real estate - the most cancerous investment vehicle in modern economies.
It extracts money from society, depletes natural resources, and does so in a way that systematically harms future generations.

Landlords leverage their wealth to buy drywall and bricks, exploiting the systemic disadvantages of younger generations, and spending their time lobbying local municipalities against high-density living and any zoning reform that might lower the value of their portfolio. They spend their Saturdays watching Graham Stephen videos on Youtube and fight frivolous lawsuits to make their teenage tenants pay for their own air conditioning.
NIMBY isn't only a disgusting personality trait. It's a disgusting financial strategy.
Forget creating a new product. Investing in a small business. Buying equities in public corporations or opening a new In-N-Out franchise (they need to come to Canada).
Instead, let’s buy a house, lobby the government to build less houses around it, and watch as its value artificially appreciates.
I wonder what happens when an entire country follows this investment philosophy?

sections.heading: Canada and Real Estate
paragraphs: If you want to see a country in financial and social freefall, look at what real estate has done to Canada.

The country's biggest "industry" is owning the dirt other people live on. We're not building factories. We're building condos for other Canadians to mortgage themselves into. The capital that should be going into machines, IP, R&D, and the kinds of companies that produce long-term, sustainable wealth is instead going into drywall, granite countertops and California shutters.
This isn't a fringe, heuristic-based cocktail I’m cooking up.

A 2024 Fraser Institute study found that an increasing share of Canada's total capital investment has gone into residential dwelling construction, while a decreasing share has gone into information technology equipment and intellectual property - exactly the opposite pattern of the United States.
The C.D. Howe Institute's 2025 report put it even more starkly: Canadian workers received only 55 cents of new productive capital for every dollar received by their American counterparts.
The result of Canada’s policies?

The unhappiest generation of young Canadians we’ve seen in decades. Canada ranks 15th on the World Happiness Index in 2024, down from 5th in 2015. For those under 30, Canada ranks 58th. The only countries with a larger fall in youth happiness between 2021–2023 are Jordan, Venezuela, Lebanon, and Afghanistan.

For context, in this time period, Afghani youth dealt with the Taliban insurgency and the Fall of Kabul. The Lebanese had a full fledged financial collapse where the Lebanese Pound 95% of its value. Venezuela had an energy state-of-emergency where they rationed electricity and Jordan was strained from repeated refugee crises.

Once the happiest age group in the country, young Canadians are now the least happy and researchers point directly to housing affordability and perceived lack of upward mobility to be the primary drivers.

The thing nobody talks about is that the housing crisis isn't an affordability problem, it’s an identity crisis. When the path to financial security in your country is "buy real estate and wait," you're telling an entire generation that productive contribution does not matter.

The kid who risks everything, lives below his means for a decade and exits from a hot startup in Toronto, and the kid from Oakville whose parents bought a lakeside property in 1998 may end up in the same financial position by 35.
Except the second kid did nothing.
He won the lottery of being born to people who happened to buy dirt at the right place at the right time.
This produces exactly the population you'd expect. Smart, educated young Canadians who feel the system is rigged.
Because it absolutely is.

This system churns out talented, young adults who spend hours researching the U.S Immigration Process, attempting to join a country where productive labour still pays. The same talented people who work hard, and watch their home country punish their work through ludicrous income/sales taxes to support social programs for boomers who hide their wealth deep in dirt.
Fixing this requires a fundamental change.

sections.heading: Henry George’s Ideas
paragraphs: In 1879, an American economist named Henry George (my GOAT economist, created Georgism) wrote a book called Progress and Poverty. It sold millions of copies and became one of the most influential economic texts of the 19th century. The core observation was deceptively simple: as cities grew richer, the people inside them got poorer. Wages stagnated, but rents exploded.
Why?
Because land is fundamentally different from every other asset. You can't make more of it. Its value comes almost entirely from what's around it, not what the owner did to it.

A vacant lot in Manhattan is worth $50 million not because the owner is a brilliant talent pushing the forefronts of humanity, but rather because eight million other people decided to build a city around it. The owner is, in the most literal sense, capturing value that other people created.
Classical economists called this the "unearned increment" -  land value that increases over time because of growth in population and improvements made by the community.
George's proposal: tax the unimproved value of land appropriately - irrespective of whatever's built on top of it.

A land value tax does a number of things. It forces land use to be productive. When you're charged a lot of money for owning land, high-density living becomes more of an economic necessity to recoup your costs. You're forced to build value and sell products to stay afloat on your investment. It also discourages speculative holding of unused land, steering capital toward uses that actually generate economic activity.
A land value tax would hammer the empty $238 million penthouse. That building's value is overwhelmingly locational - it's worth what it's worth because it's in Manhattan, not because of the marble.

But Citadel itself? The hedge fund operations, the people Griffin employs, the actual business of allocating capital? That wouldn’t be taxed. The same applies for the construction workers building 350 Park Avenue. The 15,000 jobs that project would create. That's productive activity. We want more of it.
So no taxes - according to George, that is.

When it comes to Mamdani vs Griffin, some nuance is required. The same person can be both things. Griffin-the-business-builder and Griffin-the-real-estate-collector are two different economic entities who happen to share a human form.
Our tax code can't tell them apart. A land value tax can.

The tax code should care about what you did to make your money, not just how much you made. Mamdani is right that something is broken. He's just unfairly villainizing a productive member of our society. Griffin's defenders are right that punishing job creation is dumb. They're just turning a blind eye to the fact that a $276 million dollar residence is ridiculous and not contributing to society.

sections.heading: The Implication of AI on Taxes
paragraphs: Going forward, I think we need to take a look at the way we tax labour as well.
In Canada, employer-side taxes add roughly 7-8% on top of every wage dollar. In the US, employer FICA is about the same. That's the literal tax on the act of hiring a human being.
Meanwhile, when a company buys a robot, or signs up for a Claude subscription those costs are deductible business expenses.
As AI becomes more competent and competes with humans for job openings, this is a terrible financial structure. The tax code charges you to hire a person and gives you a discount to replace them.
We're paying companies in the form of tax asymmetries that nobody talks about because payroll taxes are boring and "tax the rich" is a better tweet.

sections.heading: My Proposal
paragraphs: Now, I should be upfront: I'm broadly Georgist. I think Henry George is an absolute beauty and I share his sentiment that renting land is the great extractor of wealth from productive society.
Part of this is definitely influenced by my experience as a young Canadian having lived in Toronto & Vancouver.
But I’m not insane. And if I am, I hide it well. Hopefully.

Government spending has skyrocketed since these ideas were originally introduced, and there is no way any single tax can replace every other form of taxation. Like the Toronto Maples Leafs roster construction, it’s beautiful in theory but flames out in practice.

It would also be ridiculous for someone who makes millions of dollars a year to not pay any income tax. If you can afford to splurge on a luxury vehicle, that should probably have a sales tax on it as well. And taxing gains on equities could be done in a responsible manner without impairing economic activity.

And it’s important to acknowledge that taxes are important. They are used to fund things like basic medical care, supporting children's education and making sure that the 401 isn’t littered with potholes.
What I'm proposing is something more moderate: a shift in the composition of how we raise revenue, not a replacement of the tax system.
Keep income taxes. But reduce them significantly - especially on the lower and middle class where the marginal dollar earned represents actual productive work.

Keep corporate taxes, but structure them to reward hiring, capital expenditure, and R&D rather than passive accumulation of wealth. And then introduce a meaningful land value tax - not as the only source of public revenue, but as a major one.
The principle is simple: tax things that are extractive or scarce. Untax things that are productive and human.
This idea actually has appeal on both sides of the aisle.

Milton Friedman, every Republican's ideological godfather, famously called the land value tax "the least bad tax." An IMF working paper from 2022 found that even a revenue-neutral shift -  replacing portions of existing income/corporate taxes with land value tax revenue actually would improve economic efficiency while reducing the net tax burden on low and middle-income earners.
This isn't theoretical hand-waving by a broke 22 year old. There are real examples.

Harrisburg, Pennsylvania adopted a split-rate property tax in 1982, taxing land at six times the rate of buildings. The city was the second most economically distressed in the United States at the time.

What followed was one of the most dramatic urban turnarounds in American municipal history: vacant lots fell from 4,200 to roughly 500, over $1.2 billion in new investment flowed in, the number of businesses grew from 1,908 to over 8,800, and taxable property values surged from $212 million to $1.6 billion. All while 90% of property owners actually paid less in total tax than they would have under a conventional single-rate system.

Estonia introduced a national land value tax in 1993 by taxing the value of land only, with improvements excluded and it remains one of the most important sources of municipal funding in the country. Denmark, Singapore, and Taiwan all levy some form of land value tax alongside their broader tax systems.
None of these places abolished income taxes. They just rebalanced. And this turns NIMBYism from a lucrative strategy into a money-losing one.
And then there's the payroll side.

Eliminate employer-side payroll taxes. These are, functionally, a tax on the act of hiring a human being. Replace the lost revenue with land value taxes and, eventually, a carefully designed tax on the kind of AI/automated systems that displace labour.

To be clear, we shouldn’t tax all capital investment. But specifically, the machines/software deployed for tasks where they aren't meaningfully more productive than humans, but where the tax code makes them artificially cheaper. South Korea has already moved in this direction: in 2017, they became the first country to reduce tax deduction benefits for companies investing in automation equipment

The combined effect of these shifts would be enormous. You make it cheaper to hire people. You make it expensive to hoard land. You make it irrational to leave urban lots vacant. And you stop penalizing the person who builds a business while subsidizing the person who bought a house in 2003 and did nothing.
We should make hiring a person the cheapest thing a business can do, and make hoarding a vacant lot the most expensive.

This isn't about punishing landowners for the sake of it. It's about aligning incentives with outcomes we actually want. An economy where capital flows into R&D, into startups, into machinery and software and training - instead of into a fifth rental property in Hamilton.

The OECD, the IMF, and basically every serious productivity researcher who has looked at Canada in the last five years has said some version of the same thing: Canadian capital is being misallocated, and the tax system is a major reason why.
This isn't a left position or a right position.

The far-left wants to tax billionaires indiscriminately, including the productive ones. The far-right wants to tax nobody, including the rich landlords. Both are wrong because both are arguing about quantity when the actual problem is composition of wealth.

A moderate Georgism - income taxes that are lower and flatter, a land value tax that captures unearned local rents, and payroll tax relief that makes human labour competitive with automation is the solution going forward.

sections.heading: But Are Taxes Really That Serious?
paragraphs: One of my buddies saw me writing this, rolled his eyes and told me writing about tax policy was the “geekiest thing he’d ever heard”. He then suggested I go get plastered in a Caledon cornfield instead.
I politely declined, but that’s a pretty fair sentiment.

Tax policy, however boring and “geeky”, is a statement about what kind of society you're trying to build. What you tax, you discourage. What you don't tax, you encourage. Every line in the tax code is a tiny vote about what behaviors should exist more in the world and which should exist less.

Right now, Canada's tax code votes that owning dirt is more important than building things. Then we sit around wondering why the country can't build anything, why our productivity is collapsing, why the young people are trying to get on TN visas, and why the ones who stayed seem so quietly furious.

pullQuote: "We didn't end up here by accident. We taxed our way here."
